text:
alex: Heads up — hit a race between control-plane manifest writes and runtime reads during a hosted->dedicated fallback. App pulled old creds and failed auth. Repro below, want to align on handshake semantics.
maya: ugh. can you paste the minimal repro? :warning:
alex: repro steps:
1) create rollout that updates tenant manifest (credential change + routing policy)
2) control-plane applies manifest async and returns 202
3) runtime probe for tenant happens immediately and reads from capability cache prior to manifest reconciliation
4) request gets routed to dedicated pool, uses old creds -> 401

jun: timeline sounds like read-after-write guarantee is missing. was the control-plane write acking before durable flush?

alex: we returned once write was accepted by the api-server (not necessarily fully reconciled). The write returns quickly to keep low latency for hosted flows. The dedicated handoff assumes eventual consistency.

ria: tradeoffs: blocking write until reconciliation => +latency for management API (hosted UX hurts). Allowing stale reads => risk of auth failures on immediate handovers. Private deployments make it worse since control-plane -> runtime network could be high-latency.

sam: quick ideas:
- versioned manifests with seq numbers + runtime reject reads older than X (read-after-write by seq)
- read-after-write RPC: control-plane blocks until runtime ack (synchronous handshake)
- optimistic fallback: if auth fails, re-fetch manifest and retry (idempotent retry path)
- lease tokens: runtime only accepts traffic if it holds lease tied to manifest version

alex: example of versioned manifest sketch:
```
manifest: {
  tenant_id: "t-123",
  creds: {...},
  seq: 42
}
```
runtime read: if seq < required_seq -> force refresh from control-plane before serving.

maya: seq approach seems reasonable, but needs a way to surface required_seq to the router that initiates the handoff. otherwise router may still pick older runtime.

jun: router could advertise the desired_seq with the handoff request. e.g., router -> runtime: "serve-for-tenant t-123 desired_seq=43". runtime can NACK until it has >=43 or return a special CODE to trigger fetch/refresh.

ria: NACK path is fragile for bursty traffic. Could lead to cascading retries. Maybe combine with short-lived cache TTL + background bootstrapping so most handoffs succeed quickly.

sam: another option: control-plane issues a short-lived bootstrap token after write. Runtime validates token locally without full manifest fetch. Token ties to manifest seq and is signed. Helps Private where control-plane roundtrip is expensive.

alex: signed bootstrap token looks promising: low latency, works offline-ish, still cryptographically bounded. But needs KMS signing surface and rotation model across Hosted/Dedicated/Private.

maya: ops constraints: Private customers may reject cloud KMS; we need an option for customer-managed keys (HSM/KMS) — more complexity but doable.

ops-bot: deploy-bot: FYI there's an ongoing rollout of the manifest-change detector in staging (canary 8/10 hosts). Watch logs for "seq-mismatch".

jun: proposal for RFC follow-up:
- define manifest seq field and bootstrap token format
- router-to-runtime desired_seq header and error codes
- retry semantics and backoff for NACKs
- opt-in KMS integration for Private
- perf target: add <=20ms median to management write in worst-case (for sync handshakes we avoid if token-based)

alex: +1. Can we get a quick spike for signed bootstrap token and router header by EOW? Maya to prototype token signing; Jun to add router header; I'll wire reconciliation hook.

maya: can do. I'll open a small spike PR and add tests for token expiry and seq mismatch.

ria: also add a chaos test where control-plane is slow to ensure we don't create a SLA regression for hosted control-plane ops.

sam: I'll draft the RFC section on deployment-mode tradeoffs (latency vs durability vs offline capability).

alex: thanks all. if you see anything else in staging logs ping me. :thumbsup:
